item.title: Worshipping at the altar of Brendan Gregg (208 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://fzakaria.com/2026/11/12/worshipping-at-the-altar-of-brendan-gregg, See on Hacker News

Okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI. When you are working on a problem that has endless possibilities, it is difficult to constrain yourself to a limited set of features.

Can I just add one more?

I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables. I have been using it to help find heisenbugs, to make profile-guided optimization reproducible, and to make Nix builds bit-reproducible. But the most fun has been using it to understand performance.

Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines. I have been using it to analyze the critical path of builds.

What is the critical path?

The critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in a program. It is the minimum time that the program can take to complete, regardless of how many resources you throw at it. The only way to make a program faster is to shorten the critical path.

If you worship at the altar of Brendan Gregg, you know he spent years turning performance analysis from a dark art into a science. This is a small offering to him. 🤲

I added a new rewind time command to Rewind that analyzes a recording and tells you where the time went and what would make the run finish sooner. You can drill into any part of that answer and see the source lines responsible for it. It’s like Brendan Gregg’s flame graphs but on steroids for the critical path and with a debugger attached.11All the ideas for the command are either inspired by or directly influenced by Brendan Gregg’s work. Kneel before Zod! 

Aside: New to Rewind? Start with a flaky build you only catch once and dafuq is a deterministic VM?

Let’s see how it works by analyzing the critical path of a libuv build and test run. The build and test suite takes 78 seconds inside Rewind, and even with 64 cores it still takes 47 seconds. Why?

The usual answer is to look at a CPU profile, and in this case a CPU profile would be almost useless. For two thirds of those 47 seconds, the work the build is waiting on is not computing at all: it is asleep. 💤💤💤

§Where the time goes

Every rewind time starts with two numbers:

$ rewind time 7a29e716
libuv-1.51.0
    78.0 s  elapsed on the VM's one CPU    47.4 s  critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs            67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing

The first is how long the run took on the VM’s one virtual CPU. The second is the critical path: the longest chain of work where each step had to wait for the one before.

No number of CPUs makes a run shorter than its critical path, so the gap between the two numbers is all that parallelism can buy you.

The line under the two numbers applies Gregg’s thread state analysis. Here the biggest state is asleep: 23 seconds in epoll_pwait and 8.5 in clock_nanosleep.

A sleeping thread is invisible to a CPU profiler. Gregg’s answer is off-CPU analysis: look at where threads block, not only where they compute.

On a live machine, off-CPU analysis is hard. Linux can trace which thread woke which, and Gregg built wakeup and off-wake profiling on top of that, but you have to be tracing before the slow run happens, the tracing has a cost, and most of the sleeps you capture are noise. Rewind already logs every context switch because it needs them to replay, and now it records every wakeup and who caused it too. All that juicy information is in every recording. 🤤

Here is the whole output for libuv:

$ rewind time 7a29e716
libuv-1.51.0
    78.0 s  elapsed on the VM's one CPU
    47.4 s  critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs
            67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing

The critical path by phase
    3.54 s  configurePhase  ██
    1.67 s  buildPhase      █
    42.0 s  checkPhase      █████████████████████
     99 ms  5 other phases

The critical path by process
   on path      pid  process, with what it started
    47.4 s       34  init › bash -e source-stdenv.sh default-builder.sh
    41.9 s     4076  ├─ make -j8 SHELL=bash-5.3p3/bin/bash VERBOSE=y check
    36.4 s     4910  │  ├─ make › bash › lt-run-tests
    3.38 s     5412  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime  asleep in clock_nanosleep 3.38 s
    2.00 s     5013  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests delayed_accept delayed_accept  asleep in epoll_pwait 2.00 s
    1.62 s     5126  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_dir fs_event_watch_dir  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.62 s
    1.60 s     5103  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_close_in_callback fs_event_close_in…  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.60 s
    1.60 s     5508  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time metrics_idle_time  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.00 s, computing 600 ms
    1.24 s     6095  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests tcp_write_ready tcp_write_ready
    1.14 s     5510  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time_thread metrics_idle_time_t…  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.00 s
    1.10 s     5132  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_file_current_dir fs_event_wat…  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.10 s
    22.6 s           │  │  └─ 279 more
    5.59 s     4077  │  └─ make test/run-tests
    2.22 s     4183  │     ├─ gcc -fPIC -fstack-clash-protection -O2 -U_FORTIFY_SOURCE …
    2.10 s     4189  │     │  └─ cc1 /build/source/test/test-fs.c
    3.35 s           │     └─ 20 more
    1.99 s       68  ├─ sh ./autogen.sh
    1.99 s           │  └─ 9 more
    1.67 s     2642  ├─ make -j8 SHELL=bash-5.3p3/bin/bash
    1.67 s           │  └─ 5 more
    1.53 s      403  └─ bash ./configure --disable-static --disable-dependency-tracking…
    1.47 s              └─ 581 more

What would shorten it
    sooner      pid  if this took no time
    36.1 s           every lt-run-tests, 600 processes
    6.66 s           every cc1, 283 processes
    3.38 s     5412  75 sleeps in clock_nanosleep: lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime
    2.00 s     5013  2 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests delayed_accept delayed_accept
    1.76 s     4189  cc1 /build/source/test/test-fs.c
    1.62 s     5126  30 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_dir fs_event_watc…
    1.60 s     5103  16 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests fs_event_close_in_callback fs_ev…
    1.60 s     5508  lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time metrics_idle_time
    1.22 s           every perl, 9 processes
    1.14 s     5510  lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time_thread metrics_idle_time_thread

Look closer
  rewind time 7a29e716 --in PID             one process: its threads, sleeps and waits
  rewind time 7a29e716 --folded             the path for flamegraph.pl or speedscope.app
  rewind time 7a29e716 --perfetto F         every process on a timeline, for ui.perfetto.dev

The second table is the path as a tree of processes based on Gregg’s colony graph idea. Each line is a process with everything it started, and its time on the critical path.22A ps snapshot might miss short-lived process invocations; the recording has every fork, regardless of how brief. 

In this build, make check needs 41.9 of the total 47.4 seconds, and 36.4 of that is lt-run-tests, libuv’s test runner. The test runner invokes 287 tests each spending 1-3 seconds.

All of those tests are on the path, and the path is a single chain, so the runner ran them one after another. Worse, most of each test is spent asleep, waiting on timers.

Drag can be less than time on the path.

The last table answers a different question: how much sooner would the run finish if this part took no time? The critical path method calls this drag.

For the truly magical part, we can jump to any part of the path and see what was happening, invoke gdb and fork the run at that moment. A profiler hands you a stack, sampled at some moment you can never go back to. Every frame in rewind time is a moment in a recording, and Rewind can replay the run to it.

--in looks inside one process,33It can take a pid, a program or a word of the command line.  so let’s dive into the hrtime test that spent 3.38 seconds asleep in clock_nanosleep:

$ rewind time 7a29e716 --in hrtime
lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime (pid 5412)
    3.38 s  on the critical path with what it started, 7% of the 47.4 s path
            100% asleep (clock_nanosleep 3.38 s), <1% computing

What would shorten it
    sooner      pid  if this took no time
    3.38 s           75 sleeps in clock_nanosleep

Look closer
  rewind where 7a29e716 115894 --pid 5412   the source line the first row's time starts at  rewind time 7a29e716 --perfetto F         every process on a timeline

Since this test spent 100% of its time asleep, the step provided on the last line is where it began. rewind where replays the run to that step and asks gdb where the thread was:

$ rewind where 7a29e716 115894 --pid 5412
process 5412 (lt-run-tests), thread 5412, at step 115894
#2 uv_sleep (src/unix/core.c:1869)
    1867
    1868    do
>   1869      rc = nanosleep(&timeout, &timeout);    1870    while (rc == -1 && errno == EINTR);
    1871
arguments:
  msec = 45
locals:
  timeout = {tv_sec = 0, tv_nsec = 45000000}
  rc = <optimized out>
  __PRETTY_FUNCTION__ = <error: Cannot access memory at address 0x7fb172519ae8>
called from #3 run_test_hrtime (test/test-hrtime.c:39)
called from #4 __libc_start_call_main (../sysdeps/nptl/libc_start_call_main.h:58)

🎯 We can see that the test is calling uv_sleep(45) from line 39 of test/test-hrtime.c, and that it is sleeping for 45 milliseconds. It does that 75 times for a total of 3.38 seconds.44Turns out that the test sleeps on purpose: it is checking how far uv_hrtime moves across a sleep. There is nothing to optimize in this case. 

As the cherry on top: the run is deterministic, so step 115,894 is the same instruction every time you replay it. You can open rewind gdb at that step and investigate to your heart’s content.

The Rewind app’s Time tab shows the same answers. The path becomes a flame graph, colored the way Gregg colors his off-CPU flame graphs: computing is warm, asleep is blue, and a process shades from one to the other by how much of its time it slept.

Clicking a frame picks it and moves the playhead there, so the build log, the process tree and the files all show that moment; clicking a process again zooms into it. When you pick a blue frame, the app replays the run to that part’s longest sleep and shows the stack where it slept:

Under the stack, Show source opens the source panel at that moment on that thread, and Open gdb here opens gdb in a fork of the run at the sleep:

If you’d rather use tools you already know, rewind time can emit the data in their formats: folded stacks for flamegraph.pl and speedscope, or a Perfetto trace for ui.perfetto.dev.

The flame graph below is the real flamegraph.pl output: click a frame to zoom in, or open it on its own.

§Kneeling at the altar

Every idea here predates Rewind. Gregg has been drawing off-CPU and wakeup flame graphs for over a decade, and build systems have reported critical path information potentially even longer.55Bazel’s critical path analysis is a great example of this, and it has been around for years.  I have been inspired by his work since I first dabbled in eBPF, back when flame graphs were new. 🙇

What Rewind adds is the data. Lots of it.

Rewind has that data because it can’t replay without it. On a single CPU the only thing that changes from run to run is the scheduler, so every recording already logs every context switch.

This changes the economics of performance analysis. On a live machine, you have to trace before the run, and tracing has a cost. You can only trace a few runs, and you have to pick which ones. Rewind traces every run, so you can analyze any of them later, and do so exactly.

It has just been a manic fever joy to take ideas I have admired for years, point them at a deterministic VM, and watch them work in ways that are hard or impossible on a normal machine.

Please accept rewind time as my offering at the altar of Brendan Gregg.

item.title: Just a Few Bugs (135 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.justafewbugs.xyz/, See on Hacker News

I'm an independent security researcher. Over the years I've reported vulnerabilities to a number of vendors and manufacturers, and several of those reports have become CVEs.

For most of the past year I've been working on Google's current Pixel phones. I reverse engineered the Samsung radio stack (under embargo), the IMS and RTP media code, the Trusty trusted apps, the MediaTek M90 modem RIL and the Android telephony framework, amongst other things. In that time I filed 95 reports through the Android and Google Devices Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP), and around 95% of them came with a working proof of concept.

In total, the VRP has paid me $250, in a single payment.

I should say at the outset that I have nothing against Google. My project Box began as a fork of their AI Edge Gallery; I've worked on it most days for a year, and Google have taken features from my fork back into their own. I also maintain Iris, a hardened fork of Chromium. Much of what I do is built on Google's work. This page is solely about what happened to the security bugs I reported through their programme over twelve months.

Three things kept happening.

Bugs were fixed after being closed. For every closed report, I extracted the relevant binary from Google's current factory image and compared the exact function the report referred to. Eight had been fixed in shipped code, with a bounds check, a permission or a validation step added precisely where I'd said one was missing. All eight had originally been closed as a "duplicate" or as "not a vulnerability". None was paid and none was credited. Two more have since been fixed in the QPR3 beta.

Bugs were closed for reasons the code doesn't bear out. More than a dozen others were closed as duplicate, infeasible or "can't reproduce", yet the defect is still there, unchanged, in the current build. I'm not suggesting anyone owes a reward for a bug that hasn't been fixed, and I'm not claiming one. My point is simply that the stated reasons for closing them don't hold up once you look at the binary.

A reward promised in writing has never been paid. In January Google confirmed a valid bug and raised both its severity and its reward, in writing. Three months later they reversed all of it, with no new evidence. They then said they would "stand by our word" and pay $250 anyway as a "discretionary payment exception". That was in January. Ten months of "processing", "soon" and "no date" later, it still hasn't been paid. The report itself was submitted before December 2025.

One line in that thread still puzzles me. Google told me in writing that they were paying the Safety Center reward "even though our final technical assessment rated it as a duplicate of a report with no security impact." If the bug had no security impact, there is nothing to pay for. If it's worth paying for, then it did have an impact. Both statements are in the same ticket.

Where things stand

  • $250 Safety Center reward (Moderate). Approved in writing in January and confirmed in writing several times since. Ten months on it remains unpaid, and the ticket has been closed.
  • Two High severity reports, still "Assigned". Google formally rated both as High. Neither has a reward decision or a CVE yet. One of them has already been fixed in shipped code three times: in the QPR3 beta (DP11.261002.005) in October, in the public November stable release (CP4A.261105.040.D1, rolled out to all Pixels on 10 November 2026), and again in the latest QPR3 beta (DP11.261030.003, released on 12 November 2026). The ticket is still "Assigned" and the reward field is still empty.
  • One Moderate report, still "Assigned". Rated Moderate on 28 October. No reward decision.
  • Ten findings fixed after being closed. Each was closed as a duplicate, infeasible or not a vulnerability, and later fixed in shipped code. No reward and no credit for any of them.
  • Total received: $250.

Everything in the tables below is a closed report, and Google's wording is quoted directly from the issue tracker. I've deliberately left out the technical details of the three reports that are still "Assigned", along with anything under active coordinated disclosure.

Every report on this page is a closed ticket. Google's own position, stated on these tickets, is that they do not grant or deny permission for disclosure and that researchers are free to publish at their discretion. Nothing still under assessment or active coordinated disclosure is included here.

How I checked

I followed the same process for every closed report in the tables:

  1. Extract the exact binary, library or jar named in the report from Google's current factory image (rango and yogi Pixel builds, September and October 2026).
  2. Unpack it with the appropriate tool for the container: debugfs for ext4, fsck.erofs for EROFS, and a second pass through apex_payload.img for APEX modules.
  3. Locate the function the report cited, using symbols where they survive and, where they don't, matching byte patterns from the disassembly quoted in the report.
  4. Compare the shipped code against what the report described as vulnerable, using the NDK's llvm-objdump. The system binutils has no AArch64 backend and returns nothing without raising an error, which is worth knowing before you trust an empty diff.

Each report was given one of four verdicts: PATCHED (a check has been added that wasn't there when I reported it), STILL PRESENT (the code is unchanged), N/A (reported against this exact build, or Google described it as intended design) and CANT-DETERMINE (the binary is missing or the build doesn't match).

I didn't rely on Google's security bulletins or the supplementary patch lists. A silent fix with no bulletin entry and no credit won't appear there by definition, so the only way to find one is to compare the shipped code yourself.

The reward promised in writing that was never paid

This concerns ticket 467575499 / 470814942. On 23 January 2026 Google wrote that they had "confirmed this is a valid bug", were "increasing severity" and "increasing reward", and would "issue a payment for the new amount once it has been processed". On 24 April, without any further analysis, they reversed all three. In what they called a "Final Assessment", the same bug now "does not qualify for a reward or severity increase".

In June they wrote that they wished to "stand by our word regarding the reward". On 10 July they set out the figures: "$250 for Safety Center, $250 for the mic bug, $500USD total". They described this as "honoring our initial promise", whilst still referring to the Safety Center half as a duplicate with no security impact. The microphone half was paid. The Safety Center half was moved into a "discretionary payment exception" with, in their words, no "exact credit date". The most recent reply, in October, says much the same: still approved, still no date.

Rated High by Google, fixed in shipped code, reward still blank

Not every report ended as a duplicate or "not a vulnerability". In this case Google's own panel rated the report High severity, High quality and assigned it for remediation. The fix has since shipped three times: in the QPR3 beta (DP11.261002.005) in October, in the public November stable build (CP4A.261105.040.D1), and in the latest QPR3 beta (DP11.261030.003). The ticket is still marked "Assigned", and the reward and CVE fields are still blank, so I've kept the vulnerability itself out of this write-up. The screenshots below show only the process: a report Google rated High and confirmed in writing as eligible for a reward, then left sitting at "Assigned" after the very condition they had set had been met.

It isn't the only one. A second, unrelated report was also rated High severity, High quality by the same panel. A month later it is still "Assigned", the reward is still "with the panel" and the ASR fields are still blank. I haven't named the report or included any technical detail; the screenshots show only the rating and the state of the reward.

The duplicate ID Google admitted was wrong

When Google closes a report as a duplicate, it's closed against an internal "canonical" bug ID. I asked for the IDs behind several of mine. For two entirely unrelated bugs they gave me the same internal ID, 479203197: one was a Rust keystore panic in a trusted app, the other a C++ out-of-bounds read in the RTP media parser. They're written in different languages, sit in different subsystems and belong to different teams. A single internal report cannot be the original for both.

Google acknowledged this in writing on both tickets: "Giving you this ID for your other report was a mistake on our end," and, separately, "we made a mistake when linking the duplicate tickets." So at least one supposedly verified duplicate was marked as such without anyone checking it against the report it named.

Duplicates that appear months later, against reports I can't see

Many of my reports followed the same course. Filed, assigned, worked on by an engineer, and then, months later and with no new technical comment in between, quietly changed to Duplicate. The original is always an internal ticket I can't view, usually accompanied by a note that it was "previously reported by an internal Google engineer". I have no means of seeing that report, confirming that it exists, or confirming that it predates mine.

There are a great many of these. Of the 95 reports I've filed, 34 were closed as duplicates. A few of those are my own resubmissions and appeals folded back together, so it comes to roughly 26 distinct findings that Google accepted as real and then attributed to a report I'm not allowed to see. A duplicate isn't a rejection: it's Google confirming that the bug exists and saying someone else found it first. In 26 of my cases, that someone was an internal engineer who, by Google's account, found the identical bug in the same month I did, in firmware that had only just been released.

It's the timing I keep coming back to. I always work from the current month's factory image, so every report I file concerns firmware released that month, often only a few days earlier. When a bug I found in an image that shipped last week comes back weeks later as something Google has apparently had open internally for months, I'm in no position to check it, and it happens again and again.

On the one occasion I pressed hard enough to find out which build the original was filed against, the explanation was at least plausible. Report 549662989 was marked as a duplicate of one filed against a Pixel 10 (blazer:16/CP1A.260505.005), and PixelModemService ships the same code on both generations, so I accepted it. That was the exception. The ID mix-up described above shows what the process looks like when I can actually check it: the same internal ID given as the "original" for two completely unrelated bugs, and admitted in writing to be a mistake. If one supposedly verified duplicate was marked without anyone comparing it to the report it named, I've no reason to assume the two dozen I can't check were handled any more carefully.

The DCMO DcmoReceiver bug is a case in point. Google say my re-filed report (585012607) duplicates 545652324, which they describe as having been filed on 12 August 2026 by another external researcher, with the same root cause. I can't confirm any of that. Opening 545652324 returns "Access denied", as has every other original I've been referred to, so the date, the author and the root cause are Google's word alone. What I can check is the code, and the defect is still present and unpatched in CP4A.261105.040.D1, months after the date they give for the original report.

The "not a security vulnerability" template

Early on, Google closed one of my findings with their standard message: "not a security vulnerability, logged for potential remediation in a future version, considered closed". They later withdrew it in writing: "You are completely correct. This finding is indeed a legitimate security vulnerability. It was incorrectly closed as 'not a security vulnerability' due to an oversight during triage of this specific ticket."

The same template has since been used to close several more of my reports. On my own tickets alone it has been shown to be wrong more than once, by Google's own admission, and the issue was subsequently patched using the code I had submitted.

Closed as "Intended Behavior" by a "rate-limit bot"

From now on, whenever Google closes one of my reports, I'll publish it here. The two reports below were closed in the same way, so it's worth being precise about what happened. Both had already been assigned and triaged. A Google triager then manually moved each one back to "New", and a minute later, from the same personal account, posted a message describing itself as "an automatically generated message" from the "Google Security Bot". The message closed the report as Won't Fix (Intended Behavior) on the grounds of a rate limit, and stated "we will not be able to see any of your responses".

The genuinely automated messages on my tickets come from a separate system account. These came from the person who had handled the ticket manually a minute before, which is difficult to reconcile with an automated rate limiter. The second report was closed in this way even after I'd supplied a full reproduction on a locked, release-keys phone. Both defects can be verified directly from the shipping image.

TicketWhat it doesClosure
560456349 An app with no permissions can control the Pixel 11's carrier satellite (NTN) stack. Two exported SatelliteGateway receivers have no permission, so any app can force satellite sessions and churn gateway auth keys. ITelephony transaction 420 (overrideCarrierRoamingNtnEligibilityChanged) has no permission check, although all ~30 of its sibling methods enforce one. Its only gate is a mock-modem default that fails open: it ships as true, the only one of 11 such checks to do so (AOSP defaults to false). This lets the app pin or spoof the "carrier satellite available" signal until the phone is rebooted. Missing authorisation, Moderate. Assigned on 12 September 2026. On 16 September, "currently reviewing the technical details". On 14 November it was moved back to "New" and closed as Won't Fix (Intended Behavior), with an "automated" rate-limit message posted from the same triager account that had moved it a minute earlier. No technical assessment was given.
585028881 (re-file of 561846309) An app with no permissions can install a forged but genuinely Google-signed platform config across all eight ConfigUpdater surfaces: the emergency number database, the telephony and satellite config, the intent firewall rules, the SMS short-code list, the carrier ID database and the three TextClassifier models. The change takes effect immediately and survives a reboot. Defect A: the config signature isn't tied to the update type. PhenotypeHelper.getCertificate() returns the same certificate for every type, whereas its sibling getContentUrl() switches on type, so a blob Google signed for one type verifies for all eight (CWE-347). I proved this offline against the real production signing certificate (serial 0xcb320d3f85c0cbaf). Defect B: a cts_test_ version-skip hook with no build gate. shouldSkipVersionCheck() checks only for a file:// scheme and a cts_test_ filename, so it also fires on production user builds (CWE-1220/489). Reproduced on a locked, release-keys Pixel 6a, where an app with no permissions overwrote the live satellite config and the change persisted across a reboot. High integrity impact, and still unpatched in CP4A.261105.040.D1. First filed as 561846309 and closed as WAI. Re-filed on 12 November 2026 with a full on-device reproduction, then assigned and CLA'd. On 17 November it was moved back to "New" and closed as Won't Fix (Intended Behavior) a minute later, with the same "automated" rate-limit message from the same triager account. The same outcome as the first time, only now with the reproduction in hand.

A zero-click SMS remote code execution chain in the radio daemon, closed as "not a security vulnerability"

This is ticket 559521028. The MediaTek RIL on the Pixel 11 (libmtkmipc-ril.so, loaded by mtkfusionrild) reimplements the AOSP SMS, WAP push and 3GPP2 parsers in native C++, but keeps AOSP's habit of indexing buf[i] without checking bounds. In Java, reading past the end of a buffer throws an exception that gets caught. In native code nothing is thrown, so an over-read leaks memory and an over-write corrupts it.

There are two defects. Both can be reached with a single incoming SMS, with no user interaction and no app installed:

  • Defect A, a heap over-read that leaks data to the sender. PduParser::getAddress and constructUserData take their copy length straight from a length byte in the PDU, which the attacker controls (the TP-OA length, or TP-UDL set to 0xFF). Neither checks it against the real buffer size, so both can read up to about 255 bytes beyond the end of the PDU buffer. Those bytes are copied into the parsed message and passed up the stack, which means a remote sender can read rild's heap memory back out of the delivered message, the notification or the delivery report. That leaks heap and library pointers and defeats rild's ASLR. On this build mtkfusionrild isn't instrumented with MTE (only BTI and PAC), so memory tagging doesn't catch the read.
  • Defect B, an out-of-bounds write the attacker controls. BearerData::specialProcessForCtWapPush masks its output cursor with & 0xffff but never checks it against the 255-byte destination, and one branch uses a raw byte from the message as the memcpy length. A crafted 3GPP2 bearer data message drives the write past the end of the buffer with content of the attacker's choosing.

Use the leak to defeat ASLR, then use the write to corrupt a chosen object. That's the standard route to remote code execution in rild, the radio daemon, which runs as the radio user and has a direct channel to the baseband.

I was particularly specific about how the code is reached. The RIL does have one sanity check on PDUs, smsDeliverPduCheck, but it only sits on the branch that forwards the raw PDU to the framework. The native parser is reached by a separate path, from dispatchSms to onHandleSmsMessage to dispatchSuplMsg to SmsMessage::createFromPdu, with no check on it at all. That path depends on a SUPL gate, doesSuplExist(), which returns true for as long as rild is running on any normal device: its global is initialised to 2 in .data (confirmed in the shipped binary) and changes to 1 as soon as MediaTek's location daemon starts. The unchecked parser therefore runs on every incoming SMS, and the trigger can be a silent Type 0 SMS that the user never sees.

I re-checked both defects in three shipped builds: the October stable release (CD1A.261005.003), the November stable release (CP4A.261105.040.D1, SPL 2026-11-05) and the DP11 QPR3 beta. No bounds check had been added to any of these paths.

This is static analysis of the shipped binary. I don't have a modem test rig, as the report makes clear, so there's no runtime exploit attached. On 12 November the team asked for a live software proof of concept. Two days later, on 14 November, the report was closed as Won't Fix (Infeasible) with the template "we have investigated this issue and determined that this is not a security vulnerability... logged for potential remediation in a future version", and the ASR Severity field was set to NSBC. That is the same template Google have already withdrawn on another of my reports, here applied to an unchecked, attacker-controlled memcpy length in the radio daemon that can be reached with zero clicks and is still present in the shipping build.

Some of the other closed bugs, in plain terms

A few more of the closed reports, kept short. Each is the bug, roughly how it works, and how it is reached.

An OTA update the device will install, signed by the wrong key (ticket 541986810, closed Duplicate). RecoverySystem.verifyPackage is the check that decides whether an update package is really signed by Google. It looks at two certificates and never confirms they are the same one. The trust check looks at the certificate sitting first in the package. The signature is then verified against a different certificate, chosen by an issuer and serial number that are also read from the package. So an attacker puts Google's genuine, public signing certificate first to pass the trust check, puts their own certificate further in, points the signature at that one, and signs the package with their own key. The check passes for a package they signed. It is reached through the sideload or update path, where the signature gate that is supposed to stop an unofficial package does not.

DNS still leaves the phone when you turn on "Block connections without VPN" (ticket 552188030, closed Duplicate). VPN lockdown is meant to stop any traffic that is not inside the tunnel. DNS queries are left exempt from that block, for every app, not just the device's own traffic. So even with lockdown on, an app's DNS lookups leave the device outside the VPN, which leaks which sites are being resolved and gives a channel the lockdown is supposed to close.

Any app can switch off your Lock-on-Disconnect (ticket 552305734, closed Infeasible, still present). The Cross-Device stack exports a broadcast receiver, PermissionBroadcastReceiver, with no permission on it, and it acts on the broadcast without checking who sent it. Any installed app, holding no permissions, can send that broadcast and force an immediate un-enrollment of the user's Lock-on-Disconnect security feature, turning off a protection the user had switched on.

The share sheet fetching a picture it should not (ticket 538314136, closed Infeasible, still present). The intent resolver renders a caller-supplied icon URI without checking the caller is allowed to read it. An app hands it a URI that points at content belonging to another user or profile, and a privileged process fetches it on the attacker's behalf and hands it back.

Any app cancelling another app's on-device AI model load (ticket 558472707, closed Infeasible, still present). cancelModelLoad in the NPU manager service does not check who is calling, so any app can cancel a different app's model load and deny it the hardware AI path.

A radio service you can crash with one value (ticket 555984702, closed Can't Reproduce, still present). The grilservice radio-config path reads an array size straight from an incoming parcel with no cap and allocates it. A crafted size forces a huge allocation and takes the service down, dropping telephony.

Any app can bind the Play Store's setup service (ticket 564059393, closed Working As Intended). Play Store exports IPlaySetupServiceV2, and the permission meant to guard it declares no protection level, so Android treats it as a normal permission and auto-grants it to any app that asks. Any installed app can then bind the service. The same pattern, a guard permission with no protection level so it auto-grants, turned up across 31 exported components in the shipped image.

An unprotected "setup finished" broadcast that rewrites your system locale (ticket 563958561, closed Infeasible). SETUP_WIZARD_FINISHED is not a protected broadcast, so any app can send it. Nine privileged, system-UID receivers act on it, and one of them persistently rewrites the device's system locale. A zero-permission app sends one broadcast and changes a system-wide setting it has no right to touch.

A preinstalled app slipping past the account-ownership check (ticket 559524832, closed Infeasible). AccountManagerService.isSystemUid() actually tests whether the caller is preinstalled, not whether it is the system UID. Any preinstalled app therefore passes a guard meant only for the system, and can see and remove accounts it does not own.

Faking that you are standing next to your car (ticket 560453159, closed Can't Reproduce). Two chained UWB bugs: one leaks the secure-ranging session key, the other hijacks the Digital Key radio path. Together a zero-permission app could spoof the physical proximity that passive car entry relies on, without being anywhere near the vehicle.

One Wi-Fi frame reading out of bounds in the kernel (ticket 568933934, closed Can't Reproduce). An unsigned integer underflow in the Broadcom Wi-Fi driver's QoS-Map action-frame handler causes an out-of-bounds read in kernel heap memory. A single 25-byte 802.11 action frame from a nearby Wi-Fi peer triggers it, with no association or pairing.

A VoLTE call message that hangs the IMS stack (ticket 560878423, closed Can't Reproduce). A SIP message with a negative Content-Length is parsed as a signed value, the offset goes negative, and the receive loop never ends. One zero-click message puts the VoLTE/IMS stack into a permanent hang.

Any app reading and tampering with your Now Playing history (ticket 562215877, closed Infeasible). Private Compute Services exports NowPlayingRelayService as a binder with no caller check, unlike four sibling services in the same app. Any installed app can read and alter the record of music the phone has recognised around you.

Any app triggering a recognition pass and reading the result (ticket 561838690, closed Infeasible). The Android System Intelligence MusicRelayService binder does no caller check across its 19 transactions, so any app can read your Now Playing history and silently start a new recognition pass, listening to what is around you.

An RCS suggestion that runs JavaScript in-app with one tap (ticket 572199671, closed Working As Intended). Google Messages' blocklist for RCS suggested-action URLs misses the javascript: and data: schemes, so a crafted suggestion loads into a JavaScript-enabled bridged WebView, and one tap runs the attacker's JavaScript inside the app.

Any app reading the CBRS radio database and its coordinates (ticket 579289116, closed Duplicate). The CbsdContentProvider in SCONE is exported with no guard, so any installed app can read the CBRS CBSD database, including the CBSD location coordinates, that it should have no access to.

A Wi-Fi attribute reading out of bounds in the kernel (ticket 547477982, closed Duplicate). The Broadcom Wi-Fi driver does not validate a NAN SDEA attribute length before using it, so a crafted value causes an out-of-bounds read in kernel memory. It is reachable from a nearby Wi-Fi peer.

A system service handed the keys to start anything (ticket 558470054, closed Infeasible). dcservice, an app-tier component, is given the SELinux permission to start any init service, the only domain on the whole device with that broad grant, and for a capability its own code never uses. It is exactly the kind of over-grant that turns a small foothold into a larger one.

The SDK sandbox taking attacker file paths (ticket 561840524, closed Can't Reproduce). computeSdkStorage is the one method on the SDK Runtime sandbox service that is missing the check that the caller is the system server, so any zero-permission app can bind the service and call it with paths of its choosing.

A two-byte location message that exhausts the stack (ticket 568936058, closed Can't Reproduce). The GNSS daemon's SUPL message framing recurses into itself with no base case when a message declares a zero length, so a two-byte message drives it into infinite recursion and crashes the daemon.

A WAP-push SMS that quietly kills texting (ticket 543183960, closed Infeasible). A malformed WAP-push message lands in a loop with an empty catch block, so instead of failing cleanly the telephony process hangs and SMS silently stops working.

A SIP message body that overflows a stack buffer (ticket 540746953, closed Duplicate). The IMS SIP encoder copies a message body into a fixed 65535-byte array on the stack with no cap, so an oversized body overflows it.

An eUICC update any app can kick off (ticket 532021672, closed Infeasible). StartOtaReceiver is exported and unprotected, so any unprivileged app can trigger the eUICC OTA flow by sending the broadcast it listens for.

A system app that fetches URLs for you (ticket 537921665, closed Working As Intended). ConfigUpdater's exported receivers take a URL from broadcast extras and fetch it, with no checks, so an app with no INTERNET permission can make a system app perform requests on its behalf, a server-side request forgery.

Tethered traffic walking straight past VPN lockdown (ticket 552196751, closed Infeasible). "Block connections without VPN" does not cover tethered clients, so anything connected over USB, Ethernet or the Wi-Fi hotspot bypasses the VPN entirely. Google closed it as working by construction.

Any app repainting the real enterprise-enrollment screen (ticket 552200665, closed Infeasible). A zero-permission app can drive the phone's genuine enterprise-enrollment screen and place its own logo on it, on demand, which is the groundwork for a convincing enrollment phish.

Impersonating another process by renaming yourself (ticket 559533853, closed Infeasible). The process-monitor daemon identifies the process it watches only by reading /proc/pid/cmdline, with no UID check when the vendor config leaves the uid out. Any app can set its own process name to match the target and be treated as it.

An NFC firmware-update reply read past its buffer (ticket 537923579, closed Duplicate). The NFC firmware-update handler indexes into the response from the NFC chip using a length it does not check. It sits on the trust boundary with the physically attached NFC controller.

Any app making a system installer install an APK (ticket 563677600, closed Duplicate). WebAppService runs as a privileged app holding INSTALL_PACKAGES. By declaring a single intent-filter, any zero-permission app can make it install an APK, borrowing its install privilege.

A CDMA text message that overflows the radio daemon's stack (ticket 568929629, closed Duplicate). The MediaTek RIL's CDMA CT-WAP SMS decoder (BearerData::specialProcessForCtWapPush) writes past a fixed buffer on a crafted message, with no interaction. This is the write half of the SMS chain described above, filed on its own.

A reported heap write in the Messages image decoder (ticket 537918512, closed Working As Intended). A crafted animated-WebP image delivered by MMS or RCS, where the frame-disposal step in libframesequence was reported to clear a region using a width and height taken from the file without clamping them, overflowing the pixel buffer. Google closed it Working As Intended, and unlike most of the entries here I could not fully confirm the path in the shipped binary, so it is listed as reported and closed rather than verified.

Fixed in shipped code, closed without a reward

Each row is a closed report, checked against Google's current factory image. "Fixed" means the code the report described has changed: the report was right, the fix shipped, the ticket stayed closed and nothing was paid.

TicketComponent / functionClosureVerdict
549662989PixelModemService MintReceiver guard permissionDuplicateFixed. MINT_CONFIGURATION_UPDATE_BROADCAST now defined, signature|privileged.
538369053framework.jar PduParser.parsePartsDuplicate ("internal Google engineer")Fixed. Bounds check against stream.available() added before the allocation.
560866996framework.jar PduParser (same defect)Duplicate, "internal Google engineer"Fixed, same change as 538369053.
545948346libpixelimsmedia.so numberOfReportBlocksDuplicate, "internal Google engineer"Fixed. Underflow check added before the division.
540755547libpixelimsmedia.so decodeRtcpChunkDuplicateFixed. Bounds check on the SDES item length before the copy.
541096815libpixelimsmedia.so DecodeRtpHeaderExtensionInfeasible, "not a security vulnerability"Fixed. Length byte now read unsigned, new bounds check after it.
540753210libpixelimsmedia.so decodeRtcpFbPacketDuplicateFixed. Length check added before the op that underflowed.
529518244ShannonRcs.apk DeviceProvisioningServiceDuplicateFixed. Now requires a signature|privileged permission where it had none.

That's eight tickets, closed as duplicate or infeasible, that have been fixed in the shipping image. I re-checked all eight against the October builds and the fixes are still in place.

Two more have been fixed in the QPR3 beta (DP11.261002.005) but not yet in a stable release:

TicketComponent / functionClosureVerdict
555981160telephony-common.jar ValueParser.retrieveItemsIconIdCan't ReproFixed on QPR3 beta: a length < 1 guard added before the array allocation. Still unchanged on the current stable image.
538367541 / 543174762telephony-common.jar WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPduDuplicateFixed on QPR3 beta: a bounds check (decodedDataLength + value <= buffer length) added before the allocation. Still unchanged on stable.

The WAP push bug has now been made public

On 30 October 2026 another researcher independently disclosed a zero-click WAP push crash in Android's telephony stack (smsofdeath.com), which has been reported here: cybersecuritynews.com/zero-click-android-vulnerability. A single malformed WAP push SMS causes WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu to allocate an array from an unvalidated, truncated header length. This throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException that kills the telephony process, and because the carrier keeps redelivering the unacknowledged message, one SMS becomes a recurring outage.

I reported that exact defect twice, with the root cause in WspTypeDecoder and WapPushOverSms traced frame by frame, and a working proof against the shipped decoder:

  • Issue 538367541, filed on 24 July 2026: issuetracker.google.com/issues/538367541
  • Issue 543174762, filed on 6 August 2026: issuetracker.google.com/issues/543174762

Both were closed as duplicates of internal report 517376969, which Google say was filed by their internal automated testing in late May 2026. The fix, a bounds check before the allocation, shipped in the QPR3 beta (DP11.261002.005) and is still missing from the current stable build. On 30 October 2026 Google told me on the record that, because their internal tool found it first, my reports are "not eligible for a reward".

So in this one pair of tickets you can see the whole pattern: reported early, verified against the source, closed as a duplicate, fixed without comment in a later build, disclosed publicly by someone else, and never paid.

The fix ships before the report is resolved

The clearest way to see this is to put two factory images with the same patch level side by side. Take the WAP push crash (538367541 / 543174762, closed as Duplicate) and the SIM Toolkit crash (555981160, closed as "not reproducible" and later changed to Duplicate). Both are closed, and neither was paid.

The same file, at the same security patch level, in two builds:

  • Stable, google/yogi/yogi:17/CD1A.261005.003 (2026-10-05): still unguarded, exactly as reported.
  • QPR3 beta, google/yogi_beta/yogi:17/DP11.261002.005 (same patch level): the guard the report asked for is already there. For the WAP push bug, a bounds check before the allocation; for the SIM Toolkit bug, a length < 1 check before it.

You can compare them yourself:

jadx -d out telephony-common.jar

The bug was real enough to fix, and the fix is in a shipping build. Yet the report that found it, and described that exact fix, was closed as a duplicate or a non-issue and paid nothing. The credit went instead to an internal report I'm not allowed to see, filed on a date I can't verify, against firmware that had only just been released.

Still unpatched, closed for reasons that don't hold up

I'm not claiming payment for any of these; none of them has been fixed. They're listed because the reason given for closing each one doesn't match the code. The defect is still there, unchanged, in the current factory image. Every one of these reports has been closed.

TicketComponent / functionClosureVerdict
561846309ConfigUpdater.apk PhenotypeHelper.getCertificate()WAIUnchanged. Returns one certificate for every config type while its sibling methods switch on type.
552305734CrossDeviceAccessServicePrimary.apk PermissionBroadcastReceiverInfeasibleUnchanged. Exported, no permission.
558478942 (re-filed 585012607)DCMO.apk DcmoReceiverDuplicateUnchanged. Exported, no permission, fail-open isVerizon() carrier gate (empty operator && empty IMSI returns true, so a bogus subscription id passes it). Re-filed 12 Nov 2026 after re-verifying it in CP4A.261105.040.D1; re-closed Duplicate of 545652324, a report I can't see.
557568085TelephonyProvider.apk updateSynchronized()DuplicateUnchanged. Caller-supplied selection concatenated with no parentheses before the ownership clause.
555984702grilservice.apk RadioConfig.readFromParcelCan't ReproUnchanged. Raw readInt() size used as an allocation, no upper bound.
552188030services.jar Vpn.setVpnForcedLocked()DuplicateUnchanged. UID 0 excluded from the VPN lockdown range.
558472707service-npumanager.jar cancelModelLoadInfeasibleUnchanged. No caller-identity check, unlike sibling methods on the same class.
537920968nfc_nci.st21nfc.default.so handlePollingLoopDataInfeasibleUnchanged. Same undersized length-check logic at the function's new address.
538311587android.hardware.secure_element-service.uiccInfeasibleUnchanged. Same mutex/slot/type offsets, no per-call correlation token.
538314136IntentResolver.apk UriMetadataReaderImpl.getMetadataInfeasibleUnchanged. No ownership check on the cross-profile URI read, after a refactor.
561843639libmtkmipc-ril.so handleUssdInd(reply only)Unchanged, recompiled only. Wrong TLV length still used as the copy length.
529102332ShannonRcs.apk DebugBroadcastReceiverDuplicateUnchanged. Exported, no permission.
541986810framework.jar RecoverySystem.verifyPackageDuplicateUnchanged. The certificate checked and the certificate used for verification can still differ.
547481980services.jar FileService.enqueueOperationDuplicateUnchanged (high confidence). No ownership or permission check before dispatch.

In total

  • Fixed in shipped code with no reward or credit: eight in the stable release and two in the QPR3 beta. Ten in all, each a separate ticket.
  • Still present, after being closed for reasons the code contradicts: the tickets above, plus further Samsung and MediaTek reports submitted through the same programme.
  • Undetermined: a handful where a build or device mismatch, a missing partition or a stripped binary made the comparison unreliable. These are marked as such rather than guessed.

Similar cases

Other researchers have described much the same experience with Google's reward programmes. These are the cases that have been reported publicly.

Config Connector, 2026. In June 2026 The Register reported on Justin O'Leary's "ConfigConfusion" flaw in Google Config Connector, which allowed a user in one Kubernetes namespace to obtain organisation owner rights in GCP. He reported it on 8 March. Google replied "Nice catch!", rated it P1/S1 and accepted it, then reversed its position, said the product was working as intended and refused the reward. Google's view was that not paying a reward "does not mean that the product team won't fix the issue". Months later the ticket still showed as accepted, with no CVE and no fix. O'Leary's argument was straightforward: if it needs fixing, it isn't intended behaviour, and if it isn't intended behaviour, it qualifies for a reward.

Antigravity, 2025. When Google launched its Antigravity AI coding tool, researchers at Mindgard reported that a tampered workspace could plant code that would run every time the application started. Google closed the report on 21 November as "Won't Fix (Intended Behavior)", and only reopened and escalated it after Mindgard published their findings four days later. The issue was later fixed.

Pixel lock screen bypass, 2022. David Schütz found that he could unlock a Pixel without its passcode by swapping the SIM card and entering the PUK code. He reported it in June 2022 and, some months later, was told it was a duplicate. The earlier report was one Google had been unable to reproduce. Only after he kept pressing, and demonstrated the bypass to Google engineers in person, was it fixed in the November 2022 update (CVE-2022-20465). He was paid $70,000, rather than the $100,000 available for a lock screen bypass, because his report was still treated as a duplicate.

In 2020 CSO Online covered the wider problem (J.M. Porup, "Bug bounty platforms buy researcher silence, violate labor laws, critics say"). Critics in that piece, including legal scholars such as Amit Elazari and Katie Moussouris, argue that these programmes can be used to suppress disclosure, that researchers often have no legal safe harbour, and that the model raises questions under labour law. The description of researchers as disposable contractors whose finished work can be rejected without recourse is mine, not theirs.

item.title: Quad9 pulled their DNS service from France (315 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://quad9.net/news/blog/quad9-service-deactivation-in-france/, See on Hacker News

Back to Blog
November 24, 2026 blog

Quad9 Service Deactivation in France

(en français)

Today, November 24 2026, Quad9 will disable services for French users. This means any query reaching any Quad9 service address will be refused, and no DNS resolution will be successful. Our planned deactivation will be at 09:00 Central European (Paris) Time, to try to give users who are unaware a chance to respond quickly instead of having services down outside of normal business hours.

We are unhappy to have reached this impasse. For those of you seeing this for the first time, see our announcement of this deactivation from one month ago.

The Summary

We have received demands from beIn (a sports rightsholder company) to block various domains they claim to be related to piracy streaming sites, so users in France cannot resolve those DNS names. Currently, the courts have upheld beIn’s demands, and we have faced fines for non-compliance. We are entirely opposed to piracy, but Quad9 has nothing to do with the piracy sites. This is an attempt to force us to be part of an enforcement regime against third parties.

We have a fundamental opposition to using recursive DNS providers as a tool in this or any other content blocking campaign. Putting demands on recursive resolvers has no effect on the origin servers that deliver objectionable content. Attacking recursive resolvers is a futile and counter-productive effort, but that explanation is not understood. The policymakers and courts of France may of course make any determination they wish, even those that seem ineffective or damaging in our view. We wish to remain within legal requirements where it is necessary. We have our own strict views of what we do and what services we deliver. Because there is a mismatch between the case outcome and our mission, we must withdraw from France to remain in compliance with both law and our internal guidelines.

This is a terrible outcome, but it imposes the least amount of harm viewed over time longer than the duration of this case. We understand this will cause harm in the short term: users who do not know of our withdrawal will find our services unexpectedly unavailable. Users who have to move to different resolvers will not be protected by our cybersecurity capabilities, and they may choose to use resolvers that are less privacy-focused than Quad9.

Repeating the Obvious

We object to the core premise of the legal arguments, which is the false assertion that recursive DNS can or should be used as a method to prevent piracy or any other type of content access. Our position is this is not effective or useful, as we have no monopoly on recursive DNS, and anyone can set up their own resolver in just a few seconds (though without the privacy and malicious content protection that Quad9 offers). The courts and plaintiff have not considered this argument and ignore it entirely in the judgement. Their interest is focused on the possibility for us to do what is demanded, even if it has results outside of France, and their interest is not in why that is unjust or unwise or ineffective. So, we will continue to argue with a refutation of our ability to do this accurately without applying French law to all other European nations and the world.

How Our Withdrawal Will Work

There is an understandable focus on how Quad9 is going to block “French users” when we do not collect user information and have also claimed that geoIP blocking is insufficient for selectively denying resolution for certain names. We understand this seemingly apparent paradox, so we will expand on it as it is a question that is frequently repeated.

Our geoIP-based method to identify and deny service to French users is inexact. We are aware that our methods to geographically locate users and declare they are in France is quite imprecise - this is inevitable. By using these methods, we will create conditions of overblocking, where we accidentally classify some queries as being from France when they are not from France, and it will also result in conditions of underblocking, where we do not correctly identify some queries as being from France and inappropriately complete those requests even though the user is in French jurisdiction. This imprecision is a core component of our case: there is no legally accurate way for us to determine what queries are from users located in France versus what queries are from users not in France. But we have no other mechanism - it simply does not exist. 

These geoIP lists are inaccurate in two dimensions: firstly, IP geolocation data are often imprecise or just plain wrong, as IP geolocation is not an exact science. Mobile operators span national boundaries, corporate WANs split networks across nations, IP addresses are bought and sold frequently, and network operators shift allocations across borders. These are just a few of many other examples of how geoIP association may not be accurate. Secondly, IP location does not necessarily equate to user location, geoIP data only is a guess as to the location of the IP address, not the location of the end user. VPNs may exit in France but have the majority of their users in other nations; corporate users in one nation may egress in another due to proxies or internal DNS service distribution - there is nothing about a query that has any indication of the jurisdiction of the origin of the query itself.

The data is imprecise, but we do not know to what level it is imprecise. So we must work with what we have.

Why Not Block With This Method?

We could apply this same geoIP filter database to selectively block French users from reaching the sites we have been told to make unavailable, but this would corrupt our core premise which is that the DNS is not the right mechanism for this blocking to happen. If we comply within France to meet the requirement then we accept the worst eventual outcome for users - we lose our integrity and still do not have legally perfect coverage, plus we will inevitably apply French rulings across borders into other nations. We wish to first remain consistent with our core mission which is to only block cyber risks to end users and not content. Secondarily, we must remain as close to compliance as we can to the legal constraints put upon us. 

By accepting even the smallest of the demands for blocking based on geoIP data, we would admit that such demands are permissible within our mission - that we accept to play a complicit role in aiding companies (or others) to create ineffective and mis-directed regimes of content constraint. We would be admitting that DNS blocking is a valid instrument for the piracy problem - it is not. We would be admitting we will do this for an ever-increasing number of names - we will not. We would be permitting these methods to be applied for more areas of content filtering such as moral, religious, social, or political reasons - we must not.

So we accept there will be egregious overblocking/underblocking errors in our blockade of French users but would rather remain steadfast to our stated mission and principles to uphold the integrity of the DNS. We would rather there be a clear distinction made for users of our services: you receive the DNS as you (the user) expect, or if Quad9 is forced to pollute the service with unexpected and arbitrary number of fragmentation demands, then we will not offer the services at all.

Doesn’t Quad9 Already Block Names?

Quad9 blocks a set of cyber-threats on 9.9.9.9 (and secondary IPs) for end users, where the outcome would be an unexpected and harmful result to the end user (i.e., malicious software). Content blocking is explicitly not in that set. Quad9 has subjective editing on that set, as well - if we believe something is inappropriately categorized by our threat intelligence partners, then we can remove it at our discretion. Additionally, Quad9 also offers 9.9.9.10, which has no blocking of any kind - it is entirely open. The demands we have been given would enforce mandatory restrictions on all our service addresses, which then makes our statements of their functionality inconsistent with the reality that would be forced upon us. We will not accept that condition.

The Future Prospects

We take a long range and principled view to the outcome of this case and the others in line. There are unmistakable long-term risks to Quad9, to user privacy, and to potential fragmentation of the internet that are far beyond the current moment. To give in now would start ‘the beginning of the end’ and allow motion towards internet fragmentation that cannot be undone. We accept the risks and the pain that come with fighting where others in similar circumstances to ourselves must bend and compromise in this invisible card game where end users are not even at the table. We represent those users, and our nonprofit mission of public service is aptly unique by not representing any shareholders, products, or other interests other than the end user. 

It is especially disturbing to us to be doing this for an issue (piracy) which we believe is not slowed at all by any involvement of recursive DNS, though the damage to the integrity and trust of the global namespace is significant.

We have seen recent articles about extended blocking demands given to ISPs in France of social media or instant messaging sites, which we anticipate would be demanded of us as well if continued. It is quite clear to us the path that is being taken with these efforts: first create the mechanism, then expand the volumes of the mechanism (unconstrained rightsholder editing of the DNS), then expand the scope of prohibitions to other groups and for other reasons until there is effectively no limit to the number of editors or the reasons for DNS names to be deleted from recursive resolution. This contradicts our mission of delivery of trustworthy DNS results, and we believe this potential outcome to be antithetical to a free and open internet.

This is the second legal assault we have faced to see if the DNS can be slowly corrupted - we stood our ground and eventually won in Germany; with the continued community sponsorship and support we hope to win here, too. We refuse to take even the smallest step towards building the machinery of mandatory DNS restriction, and we will not abandon our obligation to the security, privacy, and integrity we have said we will deliver to users worldwide. We deeply regret having to step back from France and hope we will be able to return some day and offer the same unfiltered services that the rest of the world enjoys. 

Legal battles like this drain time and resources away from building a better, safer internet. Your financial support is what keeps us in the fight—and keeps our services free and open for everyone. If you stand with us, please consider donating or becoming a sponsor today.

item.title: 2035 Came Early (878 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://fzakaria.com/2026/11/23/2035-came-early, See on Hacker News

tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire, GL gears, xeyes, a voice, the weather over curl, or Firefox.

I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.

Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.

Atwood’s LawAny application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript. — Jeff Atwood, 2009

I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.

In Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev.

One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev.

It still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package, over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability. I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.

I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev

It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix.

Aside What is unkernel? It is Linux compiled to WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by Pooya Parsa on November 19th, 2026.

In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the new engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately.

The proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over qemu-wasm,11With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster.  especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The new engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload.22The benchmark page tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell. 

JavaScript & WebAssembly nirvana.

Amazingly not only does the kernel boot quickly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser.

Windows. A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by wland, and they float over the terminal you started them from.

GL. The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2.

Sound. The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser.

Network. curl, git clone and pip install work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a Wisp relay.33Thank you to @_pi0_ for adding trynix.dev to his Wisp relay allow-list. 

The best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈

Here is Firefox in trynix, and it loading trynix.dev, and then loading Firefox again inside itself.44Do not be too overjoyed. It took more than an hour for this to render. 

Sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯

2035 came early.

item.title: Making a dumb TV just smart enough (160 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://qsantos.fr/2026/11/19/making-a-dumb-tv-just-smart-enough/, See on Hacker News

I own an old, cheap TV. It has no Internet connection, no fancy smart features that make you want to install a Pi-hole, and no ask-me-again-later updates.

However, it is connected to my own desktop computer through an HDMI cable, so I can watch movies and TV series from the couch. Setting it up used to involve going to my desk, enabling the secondary monitor, opening the relevant application, moving its window to the secondary monitor, setting it in fullscreen, going back to the couch, remembering I forgot my wireless keyboard, getting off the couch, grabbing my wireless keyboard, going back to the couch again, and then pressing the Space bar.

The most important quality of a programmer is laziness.

So, of course, I vowed never to get off the couch unnecessarily. And that meant controlling everything from the TV remote.

So, I got myself an IR transmitter and an IR receiver to tinker with:

Then, I fished out an ESP32-C3 Mini devboard, a mini-breadboard, and a handful of jumper wires, and made the most basic device that could solve my woes:

I have played around with Espressif MCUs before, including for early versions of the OmniMorse, but I must admit that Claude is just faster at it than I am. With the help of Opus 5.5, I identified the RC-5 IR codes for each remote button, and set up a few scripts so that a single button press on the remote would do the whole dance I described above.

Problem solved!

But this first success unlocked much more.

I also own a bunch of old consoles. Getting everything hooked up is a chore, and makes a mess of wires. It would be much simpler to run an emulator on my computer and show it on the TV.

Thus, I installed DuckStation, PCSX2, Dolphin, Cemu and ES-DE, configured two Xbox controllers on each of them, and got Claude to start everything from a single button on the remote.

At this point, I was using two of the four colored buttons of the TV remote. So, of course, I had to come up with two more modes. I got Claude to add a Fireplace mode, which just plays 10-hour videos, the most important one being a fireplace. And also Steam, in Big Picture mode.

Soon, there were regular issues with windows opening on the wrong screen, so I switched approaches. Instead of a large desktop on two screens, I resorted to multiseat, which I had always wanted to use, with two separate X sessions, one on each screen. This also allows using both screens at the same time without interference.

But that did mean I could not directly control the windows on the TV from my regular session. So, again, I got Claude to make me an admin panel:

The virtual TV remote actually works, by sending directly through the device I cobbled together. The device also tracks volume being changed from the real remote, so things stay in sync. The rest is just commands to my computer, including a virtual gamepad, and a real-time stream of what is being displayed (mouse clicks work too!). Also, turning on an Xbox controller switches to the emulator or Steam mode, and turning the last one off goes back to the fireplace.

Last, but not least, I took a significant amount of time making (telling Claude to make) everything fast. The whole thing took me about 10 hours in total, most of which was setting up console emulators.

Claude still needs to be kept on a tight leash: it sometimes wanted to go in the wrong direction, left obvious bugs, or suggested fixes that did not address the root cause. However, it saved me a bunch of time on the original problem, and lowered the effort enough to go above and beyond!

Governor Kathy Hochul today signed a bill restricting motor vehicle manufacturers and dealers from charging consumers subscription fees after they purchase a vehicle. Amid rising consumer prices, the new law guards against a rising trend of car companies charging car owners fees to activate and use built-in features like heated seats, enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.

“New Yorkers are already struggling with rising prices due to Trump’s affordability crisis, and we’re not going to let harmful business practices increase the cost of living even more,” Governor Hochul said. “People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets.”

S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers or third-party service providers from adding subscription services or charging post-purchase fees for any motor vehicle feature that uses pre-installed components or hardware that do not have an ongoing cost. As vehicles become more advanced, the new law aims to establish clear rules preventing exploitative practices and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model.

New York Attorney General Letitia James said, “No one should have to pay recurring fees just to use features in a car they already bought. My office has secured millions of dollars for New Yorkers throughout the state who were charged illegal junk fees when purchasing a car. Unfair fees are fueling rising costs, and I am proud to work with Governor Hochul and the legislature to bring costs down.”

State Senator James Skoufis said, “People ought to know they’re able to use their already-installed remote start or heated seats during the winter without a monthly subscription. This new law will simply and clearly prohibit car manufacturers from ripping off New Yorkers who already paid for vehicle features when they purchased their car. It’s a common sense law and I’m grateful for the Governor and Assemblymember Magnarelli for their partnership enacting this legislation."

Assemblymember William B. Magnarelli said, "I thank Governor Hochul for recognizing the importance of this legislation, particularly as technology continues to evolve at a rapid pace. This law will help protect New Yorkers from unfair fees and ensure consumers aren’t paying extra for features already built into their vehicles.”

The law will take effect in 90 days on February 27, 2027.

This new law is the latest in Governor Hochul’s ongoing commitment to help address the cost of living by putting money back in the pockets of New Yorkers statewide. Under Governor Hochul’s leadership, she has:

  • Secured reforms to lower auto insurance premiums for New Yorkers, battling fraud, limiting damages paid out to bad actors, and ensuring consumers, not insurance companies, are prioritized.
  • Signed legislation requiring businesses to notify consumers of upcoming renewals and price changes as well as provide clear instructions on how to cancel subscriptions.
  • Cut middle-class taxes to their lowest rates in 70 years.
  • Tripled the Child Tax Credit, providing families up to $1,000 per child under the age of four and up to $500 for school-aged children, beginning in 2026.
  • Made school meals free for every student, saving families $1,600 per child every year.
  • Sent Inflation Refund checks to 8.2 million New Yorkers — up to $200 for individuals and up to $400 for families.
  • Increased the maximum weekly unemployment benefit by $300 a week.
